0.long_answer: Apart from the inherited genetic causes, impaired color vision can also result from a specific nutrient deficiency. In this context, vitamin A deficiency has been identified as a potential cause. Vitamin A is essential for proper phototransduction in the retina, particularly in forming rhodopsin, the photopigment required for vision under low-light conditions. When vitamin A is deficient, the visual cycle is disrupted, leading not only to night blindness (nyctalopia) but also to changes in color perception. This can result in a diminished ability to distinguish colors properly, thereby leading to impaired color vision. In contrast to congenital color blindness, which is primarily due to genetic mutations affecting the cone cells, vitamin A deficiency-induced color vision problems are acquired and potentially reversible with appropriate nutritional intervention.
